newsitem.title: CYPRUS: 16 months for diplomacy before missiles - Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: 16 months for diplomacy before missiles - Cyprus.

text.p: The Cypriot government allayed fears on Monday of imminent conflict with Turkey but said it would proceed with a controversial missile deployment in 16 months unless there was a diplomatic solution to the future of the divided island.

"What is needed right now is the concentration on efforts for a political solution to the Cyprus problem," spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides said after a U.S. envoy met Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.

Cassoulides said 16 months was ample time before the arrival of the anti-aircraft missiles -- vehemently opposed by Turkey -- for a diplomatic solution to the 23-year-old problem of Turkey occupying the northern third of the island.
However, he added: "These missiles, unless there is a decision in the meantime for a solution of the Cyrpus problem or a decision for the demilitarisation (of Cyprus), will come and be installed."
Turkey threatened military action several times last week to stop deployment of the S-300 anti-aircraft missiles, which the Cypriot government announced last week it would buy from Russia.
U.S. State Department official Carey Cavanaugh said he had not asked Clerides during their one-hour meeting to cancel the purchase, which was criticised by Washington.

"What he (Clerides) did do though, and I find this very helpful, is he gave us assurances that not a single component of those missile systems will be brought to this island in the next 16 months," said Cavanaugh, who arrived on Sunday on a mission to calm the furore.
"I believe this should effectively defuse this as a crisis issue for Cyprus. People should not now be talking of concerns of conflict because that is not a problem of today," the U.S. official said.
Cavanaugh was critical on arrival of both the Cypriot decision to purchase the 150 km-range (90 mile) missiles and Turkey's threatening response.
Cavanaugh was due to travel north later in the day across the ceasefire line dividing the island for talks with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has around 30,000 troops in the north of Cyprus, which has declared a Turkish Cypriot state recognised only by Ankara.
The Cypriot government has refused to back down on the deal, saying the missiles are needed to defend the majority Greek Cypriot-populated south of the island if there is an air raid by Turkey.
The Turkish Cypriot administration in the north of the island also threatened to move people into Varosha, a now empty tourist resort once mainly owned by Greek Cypriots but now in the Turkish zone.

Cavanaugh said on Sunday the Cyriot missile decision made a diplomatic solution more difficult: "I think it should be understood that that deal in many ways represents a setback to efforts the international community is trying to achieve on Cyprus."
But the U.S. envoy was equally critical of threats from Turkey: "There can be no justification for military action. No aggressive action here can be justified in any form."
